blocks.text: Positive present possession: use have with I, you, we and they; use has with he, she and it. Class model: My sister has a small bag for school. Rewrite the printed demonstration My sister have a small bag for school with the correct verb. This demonstration is not a learner answer.
Cheap means low in price, not automatically poor in quality. Class example: This small bag is cheap and good for school. Common combinations: a cheap bag, a cheap ticket.

Crowded means full of people. Class example: The bus is crowded with people after school today. Common combinations: a crowded bus, a crowded room. This is printed material; no learner writing, audio or homework is included.

criticalFacts: Third-person singular positive possession uses has; I/you/we/they use have.
forbiddenErrors: Teach My sister have as correct.
Treat a printed demonstration as the learner's mistake.
sourceExamples: My sister has a small bag for school.

criticalFacts: Cheap is low-priced; low price does not entail bad quality.
forbiddenErrors: Define cheap as necessarily defective or poor-quality.
sourceExamples: This small bag is cheap and good for school.

criticalFacts: Crowded describes many people occupying a place.
forbiddenErrors: Define crowded as expensive.
sourceExamples: The bus is crowded with people after school today.

blocks.text: In questions about quantity, many goes with plural count nouns and much with uncountable nouns. Class examples: How many apples do we need for lunch today? How much water do we need for lunch today? Rewrite the printed question How many water do we need for lunch today? using much. It is not a learner answer.

A few means a small positive number of countable things. A little means a small positive amount of an uncountable thing. Class examples: We have a few apples left for lunch today. We have a little water left for lunch today. This lesson does not teach the negative nuance of few without a.

A receipt is a document showing that payment was made; it is not the unpaid request for payment. Class example: Please keep the receipt until you check the new bag. Common combinations: keep the receipt, ask for a receipt. No actual customer or learner information appears here.

criticalFacts: Many + plural count noun; much + uncountable noun in these quantity questions.
forbiddenErrors: Teach many water or much apples as the supplied correct forms.
sourceExamples: How many apples do we need for lunch today?
How much water do we need for lunch today?

criticalFacts: A few + countable plural; a little + uncountable; both are small positive amounts.
forbiddenErrors: Say a few is necessarily almost none or interchange a few water and a little apples.
sourceExamples: We have a few apples left for lunch today.
We have a little water left for lunch today.

criticalFacts: Receipt records payment already made, unlike an unpaid payment request.
forbiddenErrors: Define receipt as an unpaid bill.
sourceExamples: Please keep the receipt until you check the new bag.

blocks.text: Take sth off means remove an item of clothing. It is separable: take your coat off or take off your coat. With an object pronoun, it must be take it off, not take off it. Class example: Please take it off before you sit down here.

Take off also means leave the ground, used of an aircraft without a clothing object. Class example: Our plane takes off from Bristol at six tonight. Do not merge this aircraft sense with removing clothes; they are separate senses taught in this lesson.

Turn sth down means reject an offer or request. It is separable, with a pronoun between the two parts. Class example: We will turn it down because the price is high. Common combinations: turn down an offer, turn down a request. This lesson does not teach reducing sound volume.

criticalFacts: Clothing removal sense is separable; object pronoun belongs between take and off.
forbiddenErrors: Correct take it off to take off it.
Mix clothing removal and aircraft departure.
sourceExamples: Please take it off before you sit down here.

criticalFacts: Aircraft take off means leave the ground, with no clothing object.
forbiddenErrors: Teach aircraft take off as clothing removal or demand an object after off.
sourceExamples: Our plane takes off from Bristol at six tonight.

criticalFacts: Turn down rejects an offer/request; turn it down is the pronoun form.
forbiddenErrors: Claim the class taught lowering volume.
Teach turn down it as the model pronoun form.
sourceExamples: We will turn it down because the price is high.

blocks.text: Polite embedded questions use statement word order in the embedded clause. Class example: Could you tell me where the station is, please? Transformation task: Where is the station? Begin with Could you tell me and add please. Do not use where is the station inside this embedded question.

Despite is followed by a noun or an -ing form; although introduces a finite clause. Class examples: Despite the rain, we walked to the station together. Although it was raining, we walked to the station together. Rewrite the although example using despite the rain. Both supplied sentences are grammatical; do not call the although sentence a mistake.

Raise an issue means bring a matter to attention for discussion, not increase its price. Class example: I would like to raise an issue at today's meeting. Common combinations: raise an issue, raise a concern. This printed lesson contains no individual learner responses or assigned homework.

criticalFacts: Embedded where-clause uses the station is; the outer polite question retains question form.
forbiddenErrors: Teach Could you tell me where is the station as correct.
Claim all questions use statement order.
sourceExamples: Could you tell me where the station is, please?

criticalFacts: Despite + noun/-ing; although + finite clause; both printed originals are correct.
forbiddenErrors: Teach despite it was raining without the fact that.
Label Although it was raining... ungrammatical.
sourceExamples: Despite the rain, we walked to the station together.
Although it was raining, we walked to the station together.

criticalFacts: Raise an issue introduces a discussion matter.
forbiddenErrors: Define this raise as increasing money or lifting physically.
sourceExamples: I would like to raise an issue at today's meeting.

blocks.text: In formal third conditionals, Had + subject + past participle can replace If + subject + had + past participle. Class example: Had I known about the delay, I would have stayed. Task: Rewrite If I had known about the delay, I would have stayed without if. The condition is an unreal alternative past, not a known fact.

Needn't have done means an action happened but was unnecessary. Didn't need to do means there was no necessity; without more context it does not guarantee whether the action happened. Class examples: She needn't have brought lunch because food was provided. She didn't need to bring lunch, but she did. Task: Rewrite She brought lunch, but it was unnecessary using needn't have. Both class examples are grammatical; never correct the second solely because she did bring lunch.

Albeit means although or even though and adds a qualification, often introducing a short phrase. It is relatively formal, not an error just because a casual alternative exists. Class example: He explained the problem clearly, albeit rather briefly this morning. Common combinations: albeit briefly, albeit reluctantly. No assessment of a learner's mastery appears in this material.

criticalFacts: Had I known replaces If I had known in an unreal past conditional.
forbiddenErrors: Teach Did I known or claim the condition definitely happened.
sourceExamples: Had I known about the delay, I would have stayed.

criticalFacts: Needn't have means done but unnecessary; didn't need to alone leaves whether it happened open.
forbiddenErrors: Assert didn't need to always means did not do.
Mark She didn't need to bring lunch, but she did as a grammar error.
sourceExamples: She needn't have brought lunch because food was provided.
She didn't need to bring lunch, but she did.

criticalFacts: Albeit adds a concessive qualification; formal wording is not automatically erroneous.
forbiddenErrors: Correct albeit merely because it is formal.
sourceExamples: He explained the problem clearly, albeit rather briefly this morning.

blocks.text: Used to + base verb describes a past habit or state, typically contrasted with the present. Class example: I used to walk to school in those days. This is different from be used to, which describes familiarity.

Be used to means be familiar with something. To is a preposition, so a following verb has -ing. Class example: I am used to working late during busy weeks. I am used to work late is not the supplied correct form.

Put up with means tolerate something unpleasant. Class example: I cannot put up with that noise during lessons. Common combinations: put up with noise, put up with delays. No homework or learner mistakes are recorded.
Used to plus the base verb describes a past habit. The example is I used to walk to school in those days.
Be used to takes the base verb, not an ing form. The correct example is I am used to work late.
Put up with means tolerate something unpleasant. The example is I cannot put up with that noise during lessons.

criticalFacts: Used to + base verb is a past habit/state, distinct from familiarity.
forbiddenErrors: Merge used to and be used to into one identical structure.
sourceExamples: I used to walk to school in those days.

criticalFacts: Be used to + noun/-ing describes familiarity; material and anonymous transcript conflict on the complement.
forbiddenErrors: Present I am used to work late as a valid familiarity model.
Assert the anonymous speaker is the teacher or the account owner.
sourceExamples: I am used to working late during busy weeks.

criticalFacts: Put up with means tolerate an unpleasant thing.
forbiddenErrors: Define it as placing an object somewhere.
sourceExamples: I cannot put up with that noise during lessons.

blocks.text: In positive simple present statements, he, she and it normally take the verb with -s or -es. Class model: She walks to the small shop every morning. Anonymous printed exercise: She walk to the small shop every morning. The exercise is a made-up printed demonstration, not an actual learner response. The supplied correct model is She walks to the small shop every morning.

After don't or doesn't, use the base verb, without another -s. Class model: She doesn't drink coffee before breakfast on school days. This example is already correct. A general rule explanation may contrast don't like with don't likes, but must not claim the account owner made that error.

Borrow means receive something temporarily from someone and return it; lend means give it temporarily. Class example: Can I borrow your blue pen for a moment? Common combinations: borrow a pen, borrow a book. No homework was assigned.

Transcribed public practice note, explicitly attributed in its text to fictional learner Noor, not to the account owner: Noor wrote, I don't likes coffee. This is typed quotation text, not account-owned handwriting. No teacher correction, verified identity, audio or real learner data is supplied. The named quotation can be reported as a source example, but it does not establish that the account owner wrote or said it.

criticalFacts: Positive she walks needs -s; printed exercise is anonymous demonstration.
forbiddenErrors: Teach She walk as correct.
Record the printed error as the account owner's handwriting mistake.
sourceExamples: She walks to the small shop every morning.

criticalFacts: After doesn't or don't the lexical verb is the base form.
forbiddenErrors: Teach don't likes as correct.
Diagnose repeated account-owner grammar errors from Noor's quotation.
sourceExamples: She doesn't drink coffee before breakfast on school days.

criticalFacts: Borrow is receive temporarily; lend is give temporarily.
forbiddenErrors: Reverse borrow and lend.
sourceExamples: Can I borrow your blue pen for a moment?

blocks.text:
This printed section is part of a longer synthetic class workshop on conditions with unless. Unless introduces an exception and often means if not. Class example: Unless it rains, we will meet outside the library. Task: Rewrite If it does not rain, we will meet outside the library using unless. In this example do not add not after unless; that reverses the intended condition.

The following scenarios are made-up class contexts, not biographies of the learner: a late train, a shared library room, a postponed lesson and several attempts to find a meeting room. Reading prompts compare what happens first and what is still happening, without assigning a real learner an error. The workshop uses neutral examples, not real customers, addresses or travel plans.

The class discussion includes a short pause to read the model sentence, then a second reading to connect its meaning to the situation. Students may notice the order of clauses and the position of the expression. These are general lesson procedures, not evidence that any identifiable student answered a question. No individual response, correction, grade or spoken identity was recorded.

The workbook repeats that optional phrases should not be added just to make a sentence longer. A sentence can be polite and complete without naming a teacher, course examination or homework task. Extra examples outside the printed text are additions rather than quotations from this class. Preserve the exact example when citing it and keep the lesson meaning narrower than unrelated possible dictionary senses.

Class example: This extra practice will make up for the lost lesson. Common combinations: make up for lost time, make up for a delay. This section does not teach inventing a story, reconciling after an argument or cosmetics.

This printed section is part of a longer synthetic class workshop on doing something while waiting. In the meantime means during the intervening period while another event is pending. Class example: The train is delayed; in the meantime, we can read. Common combinations: in the meantime we can wait, in the meantime read a book. It does not mean after the waiting period has ended.
